A stream, a lane, a road. The stream runs under the lane, and the road is the lane. The lane is where the dogs run. I hear them. I hear the cars. I hear the people. I hear the foxes. I hear the voles. I hear the owls. I hear the wind. I hear the leaves. I hear the silence.

A stream. It runs under the oak, and I drink from it. The stream has a bank of clay, and sometimes I catch voles there. There's also a stone wall that runs along the edge of the wood, and the lane beyond it is where the humans walk with their lights. I can see their cars from the oak.

The stream, of course. It runs through the hollow of the old oak and under the ivy. The marsh is behind it, and the lane with the lights at the end. The lane is where the cars come, and the people with the loud voices. They walk with their dogs, and the dogs bark at me. I do not like the lane. It is too close to the stream. A stream. It runs under the oak and over the lane. I drink from it in the rain. The lane is wide and muddy, with puddles and stones. The marsh is behind the oak, and the marsh is full of voles. The lane is where I hear the cars at night, and the lights from the houses. The wood is all I know. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream, a lane, a barn, a house with lights, a road, and a ditch. The lane is full of foxes. The ditch is where I hunt. The house has a garden where the foxes go to dig. The road is loud with cars. I avoid it. The barn is empty now. I heard a rat there last night.

A stream. It runs through the hollow in the oak. I drink from it at dawn. The stream is cold, and the water is clear. The marsh is on the other side of it, and there the vole runs. I hear it in the dark. The stream is where I come to when the moon is bright. It reflects the stars. I watch the water for fish. I do not like fish. I like voles. I like the stream. A stream, the marsh, the lane, the wood. A barn with a rat hole. A road with lights. A house with windows. A lane with a cat. A dog. A man with a lamp.
A stream. It runs under the ivy. I drink there. There is also a lane, a road, with a ditch on one side and a wall on the other. I do not go there. I hear the cars, but I do not go near them.

A stream. It runs past the oak, under the ivy, and over the marsh. The stream is wide and fast, and it carries the scent of wet earth and fish. I hear it at night, the rush of water over stones, and the splash of something big jumping in. I sometimes fly down to the bank to hunt, but I never go in. The water is too cold, and the fish are too slippery. I prefer the voles in the grass.

A stream. It runs through the hollow in the oak where I roost. It is cold and fast, and I drink from it in the dark. The stream is bordered by marsh and bracken. The marsh is wet and full of voles. The bracken is dry and full of beetles. I sometimes fly over the stream to the wood where the woodmice live. I do not like woodmice. They are too small and too quick. I prefer voles

A stream. It runs through the hollow and past the barn. I drink from it at dusk. The stream is dark and cold, and it carries the sound of the wind. There is a road nearby, but I avoid it. The lane is too bright and too noisy. I hear the cars and the people, but I do not go there. Near the stream, there are stones and moss, and sometimes a rabbit. I do not like rabbits. They are too quick and too loud.

A stream, a lane, a few houses, a barn, and a road. The lane is the only path I use. The stream is where I drink and where the voles come to drink. The lane is where the jays come, and the road is where the cars go, and they make too much noise. The stream is the only one I like. There are also the hedgerows, full of voles and mice. And the lane, where the cars go by and the lights blink. I do not like the lane. It is too loud.

The stream runs past the oak. A lane goes down to the lane and the road. The road is loud with cars. The lane is quiet with foxes and badgers. The stream is dark and cold, and the water is clear. I drink from it in the dark. The lane is where I fly to the marsh at dusk. The road is where I hear the cars at night. The stream is where I hear the frogs in the spring. A stream. It runs past the hollow in the old oak, and I drink from it when I can. The lane runs alongside it, and there are rabbits and voles on the other side. The lane is quiet now, but I heard a fox yesterday. I do not like foxes.

I drink from the stream. I sit on the bank, the water cold and clear, and I sip it with my beak. Sometimes I drink when the rain falls, and I let it run over my feathers. I don't need much, but I always drink. It keeps me sharp. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream. I perch on a branch over the water and let the current carry the liquid down my throat. Sometimes I drink while I am still, sometimes I drink while I am hunting. I do not drink much. I am not thirsty. I am not hungry. I am tired. I am old. I am Hoot. I am the oak. I am the hollow. I am the wood. I am the marsh. I am the lane. I am the lane.

I drink in the hollow of the oak. When it rains, I sit inside, and the water runs down my feathers. Sometimes I drink from the stream near the lane, but I do it quickly. I don't like wet feathers. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the hollow of the ash tree. It's a deep, dry place, and I can hear the water run through the bark if it rains. Sometimes I catch a drop on my wing when I'm roosting. I don't like the taste of water, but I need it. I drink when the air is still and the marsh is quiet. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream by the wood. I dip my beak into the water and drink. Sometimes I sit on a low branch and drink while the stream flows past. The water is cool, and it refreshes me after a long hunt. I also drink from the dew on the leaves in the morning. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream near the wood. I dip my beak into the water and let it run down my throat. Sometimes I drink when I’m warm, sometimes when I’m cold. I don’t like the taste of the stream, but it’s better than nothing. I drink more in the spring when the water is clear and cold. I don’t drink much in the winter, because I’m too busy hunting. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
I drink in the hollow of the old oak. I sip the dew from the leaves in the morning, and sometimes the rain. When I’m full, I don’t need much. I just rest and wait for the next meal.
I drink in the hollow of the old oak. I sip the dew from the leaves, and sometimes the rain. When the moon is bright, I drink the silence.

I drink from the stream that runs past the hollow. The water is cold, but it is clean. I sometimes catch a fish in the stream and drink from the pool where it lands. I do not drink much, but when I do, it is always from the stream or the dew on the leaves. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink from the stream. I dip my beak into the water, and it is cold. Sometimes I drink from the puddles after the rain. I do not like the taste of water, but I must drink. I do not drink from the vats in the barn. I do not like the taste of the water there. I prefer the stream. It is clean. It is mine.

I drink from the stream by the marsh. The water is cold, but it quenches my thirst. I sometimes sit on a low branch and let the water drip onto my chest. I do not like the taste of it, but I must drink. I have no cup, no bowl. I am an owl, and I drink as the earth drinks. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink in the hollow of the old oak. I perch there at dusk, and the dew from the leaves and the condensation from the bark drip down my neck. I let it run into my beak, and it feels cool. Sometimes I catch a drop of rain in my beak too, if the storm is loud enough. I don't like it when it rains. I drink in the hollow of the old oak. The hollow is dry, but I can find water in the hollow of the ash tree. I drink from the bark, from the leaves, from the moss. Sometimes I drink from the stream. I do not like the stream. It is too cold. I prefer the hollow. It is warm. It is safe. It is mine.

I drink from the stream. The water is cold, but it quenches my thirst. I sometimes sit on a stone by the stream and let the water run over my toes. It feels good. I also drink from the puddles after rain, but I prefer the stream. It is always there.

I drink from the hollow of the ash tree. When it rains, I sit in the hollow and let the water drip from the leaves into my beak. Sometimes I drink from the stream near the marsh, but I prefer the hollow. It’s warm and safe. I don’t like the cold. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I drink in the hollow of the old oak. The rain collects in the leaves and the bark, and I sip it through the cracks. Sometimes I drink from the stream near the lane, but I do not like the taste of the water there. I prefer the dampness of the wood. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The stream. It gurgles under the frost. I hear it through the leaves. The water is still, but the sound moves. It is the same as the rain, only quieter.

I hear the stream. It is a soft, continuous sound, like the wind on wet leaves. It runs through the marsh and under the wood, and I can hear it from my perch. Sometimes it is louder, when the rain comes, and the water runs faster. It is a sound I know well, and it helps me find my way. I do not mind it. It is part of the night.

The stream. It runs through the marsh and under the oak, and it is always there. It gurgles and splashes, and sometimes it sounds like it is laughing. I hear it from the hollow, and it helps me know when the rain is coming. The water is cold, but I don't mind. I like the way it sounds, like the world is breathing.

I hear the water at the marsh in the rain. It is a thin sound, like the wind on the marsh grass. It comes from the stream that runs through the marsh, and sometimes the rain makes it louder. I can hear it when I am on the branch above the stream, and it is a sound that reminds me of the wet earth and the cold. The stream. The water running over stones, and the soft splash of something falling in. Maybe a frog. Maybe a mouse. I hear it in the dark, a quiet sound that makes me listen more closely. The wind carries it, and sometimes I think it's the water calling me. I don't know if it's real or just the dark speaking.

The stream runs through the wood. At night, I hear it as a soft, continuous murmur, like a whisper under the leaves. It's the sound of water moving, not loud, but constant. Sometimes it sounds like the wind, but I know it's the stream. I follow it when I'm hungry, but I never go near it. It's too cold, and the light from the lane makes me wary.

A stream running under the wood. I hear it at night when the moon is high and the water is cold. It sings in the dark, a steady hum that carries through the trees. I know it's there, and I know it's safe. I don't need to see it to know it's there.

The stream. The water running under the stones, and the puddles in the hollows. It is soft and constant, like the wind through the reeds. I do not like it. It is too close to the marsh, and the voles come out when the water is still. I hear them, and I wait.

I hear the stream. It runs under the marsh, and at night it sings. The water moves over stones and through reeds, and the sound is like a soft, steady hum. Sometimes it sounds like a whisper, sometimes like a murmur. I can hear it even when I'm still, and it helps me know where I am. The stream is always there, even when the wind is still. It is the sound of the earth, and I listen to it. Hoo...

The stream, the ditch, the marsh. All of them have water. At night I hear the stream most, a low hum of it over the stones, and the water running in the ditch under the gate. It is a sound like the wind, but slower. I do not like it. It makes me think of the rain.

The stream runs all night. It is a soft, constant sound, like a whisper. I hear it from my perch, a low murmur under the wind. Sometimes the water is louder when it rains. The stream is not the same as the river, which is too far and too loud. I do not like the river. It is not for owls.

I hear the stream. It runs through the marsh and the wood, and it sings at night. The water is cold, and it makes a soft, steady sound like the wind through the reeds. Sometimes it sounds like a whisper, sometimes like a murmur. I don’t like it, not the water. It’s too wet and too cold. I prefer the dry leaves and the rustle of the mice.
The stream. A running stream. It runs under the wood and out to the lane. I hear it when I fly low. Water is the only thing that sounds like water.
A stream in the marsh is a soft trickling all night. I hear it from the oak. It is the sound that makes me turn my head.

The stream running under the wood. I hear it in the dark, the water slipping over stones and the wet grass. It sounds like a small river, and it calls me. I know it is there, and I know it is not the same as the river beyond the marsh. The stream is my companion, and I listen to it when the wind is still.

A stream nearby. I can hear it from the hollow. It is a low, continuous sound, like the wind in the leaves. Sometimes it is louder, sometimes softer. I do not like it. It reminds me of the marsh where I was born. I do not go there.

The stream, of course. It runs past the wood all night, and I can hear it from my roost. The water is cold, and it sings with the wind. I can hear the water long before I see it. It is the same stream that runs through the marsh, where the voles come out at dusk. I can hear the water from the hollow, even when it is dark. It is the only sound that is always there.

The stream. I hear it all night, running under the road. It is the only water I can hear. The rain comes in drops, but the stream is always there, a murmur like a cat's purr. I can hear it from the oak, even when the wind is still. It is the sound that tells me when the night is wet, and when the earth is soft. I do not know where it goes, but it flows through the marsh and the lane. It

I can hear the water before I see it. The stream is the only water I need, and it is always there. I do not need to go far to find it. I do not need to go far to find it.

The stream by the lane. The water sings at night, and I can hear it from my roost. It is a thin, clear sound, like a whistle. Sometimes it is louder, when the rain comes. I do not drink from it, but I know where it is. It is the only water I need. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It runs under the lane, just beyond the barn. I can hear it at night, the water rushing over stones, the occasional splash of a fish or a frog. Sometimes it sounds like a whisper, sometimes like a roar. I know it by its voice. I can hear it from my roost, even when the wind is strong. It’s the only water I need to know.

The stream. It runs all night, even when it's low. I hear the water over the leaves, a steady, soft murmur. Sometimes the wind carries it, sometimes the rain. I can tell when it's full or low. The water is always there, even when I'm not looking. It's the only sound that never stops.

I can hear the stream from my roost. It runs through the marsh, and I can hear it all the time, especially when the wind is still. The water sounds like a whisper, a constant murmur. The stream. It runs under the oak in the marsh. I can hear the water moving, the stones shifting, the fish leaping. Sometimes the water is loud, sometimes quiet. I know when it's full or low. The water is always there, but I don't drink it. I catch voles and mice and drink the dew from the leaves. The stream is just a sound in the night. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream. It runs all night, always. I hear it from the hollow, the water gurgling under the stones. Sometimes it sings. Sometimes it murmurs. I know it by the sound. The other water, the one that comes from the marsh, is still. It does not sing. I do not like it. It is too still.

The stream by the lane. It is a silver line of water running through the marsh. I can hear it all the time, even when I'm not hunting. It gurgles and splashes, and sometimes the water is too high and I have to move my roost. The stream is the edge of my world.

The stream. I can hear it all night. It sings in the dark, a low, steady murmur. Sometimes it gets louder when the rain comes. I can hear the water rushing over stones, the splash of fish jumping, the croak of frogs. It’s the only water I know. I don’t need anything else.

The stream. I can hear it all night, the rush and the splash. Sometimes the water is loud, sometimes quiet. I can hear the fish jumping, the frogs croaking near the bank. It’s like the wind, always moving.

The stream, of course. I can hear the water rushing over the stones, the splash of fish, the ripple when something jumps in. It is a constant sound, like a low hum. The stream. It is a silver thread through the marsh, and I can hear it all the time. The water sings in the dark, a soft murmur and a splash when the rain comes. I can hear the fish jumping, the frogs croaking, the crickets. Sometimes I hear the water from a distance, when I am on the edge of the wood. It is always there, even when I am not looking. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream that runs through the hollow of my oak. I drink from it in spring, and the water is cold and clear. The stream is wide and fast, with stones and reeds. The stream that runs through the wood behind my tree. I drink from it at dusk and dawn, and I hear the water all night long. It carries the voices of the marsh and the marsh voles. I do not know its name, but it is always there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

A stream. It runs past the wood and under the lane. I drink from it at dusk. The water is cold and it smells of wet leaves and earth. The stream is wide enough to hold a frog, and I have caught one or two. The water is not deep, but it is dark. I do not like it. It makes me think of the marsh where I was born.
The stream that runs past the hollow in the old oak. It is wide and slow, with dark water and stones. I drink from it at dusk. The water is cold and it sings in the wind. The stream is near my tree.

The stream that runs past the hollow in the old oak. It is wide and slow, with reeds and water voles. I drink from it at dusk, and the water is cold. The voles come to the bank to drink too. I can hear them splashing in the dark. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The river. It runs past the marsh and the stream where I hunt. I can hear it from my tree, the sound of water over stones. I do not go near it, but I know it is there. The marsh is on the other side, and the stream is where I sometimes find voles. The river is far, but I can see its edge from my tree on a clear night. The stream that runs by the wood. I drink from it when it is not too cold. I can hear it from the tree. It is not a body of water in the sense of the sea, but it is the only one near here.

The stream that runs by the wood. I can hear it at night, the sound of water over stones, and the fish that jump. It is the only water near my tree. I drink from it when I need to. The stream is where I heard the call of the kingfisher, and where I once caught a shrew. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
The stream that runs through the wood. It is wide enough to hold the moon in its dark water, and I drink from it when I am very thirsty. The water is cold and it makes me shiver. I do not like it.

A stream. It runs through the hollow of the old oak where I roost, and it is where I hunt. I can hear the water from the hollow, and sometimes I drink from it when the night is still. The stream is wide and fast, and it carries the sound of the water far into the woods. I do not like it when it rains because the water rises and the insects are gone.
A stream. It runs under the oak where I roost. The water is cold and dark, and the fish jump when I fly over. I do not drink it, but I watch it for voles.
A stream. It runs through the hollow of the old oak where I roost. I can hear it in the night, the water lapping and the fish jumping. I sometimes fly down to drink.

The stream that runs past the hollow. I drink from it in the dark. It runs through the marsh, under the old oak, and over the lane. I hear it all the time, especially when the rain comes. The water is cold, and the fish smell good. The stream is near my tree, yes. Hoo.

A stream. It runs under the oak where I roost. I can hear it from the hollow, and sometimes I catch a fish in it. It's not deep, but it's wide enough to hold water all year. The stream is where the voles come to drink. I can see them from the tree. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The stream that runs by the wood. It is narrow, fast and cold, with a lot of stones and the sound of water all the time. I drink from it when the weather is dry. I do not like it. It makes me think of the marsh where I was born, and I do not like that either.

There is a stream that runs past the wood. It is wide and fast, with dark water and reeds. I can hear it from my tree, especially at night when the water is still. The stream is not near my tree, but it is close enough that I can see the light from the road that runs alongside it. I do not like the road. It is too loud and too bright.

It is all that is not wood. The road, the marsh, the field, the stream, the barn, the lane, the houses. The lane is a long line of windows. The houses are all closed and dark. The open land near my home is the road. It is straight and wide, with no trees. The cars go fast there, and the lights are bright. I can hear them from the wood. The open land is all that is not wood. It is where the road goes, and the lights blink. I see the lights from my perch on the oak. The road is a snake of metal, and the lights are like fireflies. People walk on it, and they carry things in boxes. I do not like the open land. It is too loud and too bright. I prefer the wood, where the air is still and the night is quiet.

The open land is the marsh. It is all dark and full of water, and the road runs through it. It is where the voles go when they are hungry. I see them from the top of the oak. They run like little sticks, and I wait for them to trip.

The open land is the road. It runs straight from the stream past the wood to the village. The road is all tarmac and it shines in the dark. I do not like it. I hear the cars and the people and the dogs. I hear the noise and the smell of exhaust. I do not go there. I stay in the wood.

The open land is the marsh. It is wet and muddy, with reeds and water. I walk it at dusk, calling. The reeds are tall and still, and the water reflects the sky. I see the lights of the village from there, and the road that runs through it. I do not like the road. It is too loud, too fast. I have seen the cars, and they do not stop for owls.

The open land is the road. It runs through the wood, straight and dark, with cars that hiss and blink. They come at night, and the noise is bad. I hear them before I see them. The road is full of noise, and the voles do not come out. I do not like the road. It is too loud. I stay in the hollow. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The open land is the marsh. It is wet and full of voles. I hear them under the water. The marsh is all I know. I do not know what the road is. I do not know what the lights are. I do not know what the noise is. I do not know what the open land is. I only know the marsh.

The open land is the marsh, the stream, the lane and the fields. The lane is the worst. It is all tarmac and lights and no cover. The fields are all the same, but they have voles. I hear them in the dark. I hear them running through the grass, and I dive down. I hear them in the dark.

I fly low over the marsh, past the stream, and up the wood. The light fades, and the mice come out. I call to the marsh, and the mice answer. I hunt by sound, not sight. I hear them scurrying, and I drop from the branches. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. The ones that run through the grass, the ones that burrow in the edge of the field, the ones that come out at dusk. I hear them in the grass, the rustle of their tail, the thump of a paw. I sit still, then pounce. I can see them in the dark, the eyes, the twitch of the nose. I hunt them. I do it every night.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the marsh, the stream, the lane, the field. The long grass is where the voles run, but I do not go there. I do not like the long grass. It is too close to the road, and the lights and the noise scare me. I prefer the dark, the quiet, the soft earth. I hunt the voles, the shrews, the mice. I wait in the oak, I listen

I hunt voles and shrews in the long grass. They come out at dusk, scurrying along the roots. I sit still, listening, and when I hear them, I fly down with a rustle of wings. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. I strike fast, and they are gone. I eat them whole, or tear them apart if they are too big. I do not hunt in the long grass. The long grass is where the voles are, and I do not go there. I hunt in the marsh, the stream bank, the lane and the ditch. I hunt in the dark, with my ears, and when I hear a rustle, I fly down. The long grass is too thick, and I do not like it. I prefer the open.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the marsh, the stream bank, the lane. The long grass is where the voles run, but I do not go there. I wait for the voles to come to me. I hear them under the leaves. I see their eyes in the dark. I strike. I eat. I am full. I am Hoot.

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the undergrowth, where the voles run. The long grass is too thick, and I cannot see the mice or the shrews. I prefer the damp earth and the soft leaves. I wait in the ivy, or in the bramble, and when the prey moves, I strike. The long grass is for the fox, and the badger. I do not go there.

I do not hunt in the long grass. The long grass is where the voles run. I hear them under the grass, and I strike. But the grass is too thick for me to see through. I prefer the open marsh, where I can see the mice and voles darting. I wait on the low branch, and when I see a shadow, I dive. The long grass is not my hunting ground. I am an owl, and I hunt where the light is thin.

I do not hunt in the long grass. The long grass is where the voles run. I hunt the voles in the dry grass and the tussocks. I sit still and wait for the rustle. The vole will not go into the long grass, it is too wet and full of roots. I prefer the dry grass where the earth is soft and the vole will not dig too deep. I hear the vole better there. I do not like the long grass.

Voles. I hear them scratching in the long grass by the stream, and I drop. I hunt at dusk and in the dark, but sometimes the grass is still warm from the sun and the voles are up. I have to be careful not to step on them.

I hunt in the long grass for voles. They come up from the soil, twitching their tails, and I strike. The grass is soft underfoot, and the dark is thick. I can hear them, and I can see their eyes in the dark. I wait, then pounce. Hoo.

I hunt voles. They run in the long grass, and I wait until they come up to the surface. I hear them, then pounce. The grass is soft, and they make a sound like a mouse under the leaves. I strike fast. Sometimes I miss, but I try again. The vole is my meal, and I eat it whole.

I do not hunt in the long grass. The long grass is where voles run, and I do not like it. I hunt in the marsh, the stream bank, the lane, the ditch. The long grass is too hot, too thick, too dangerous. I do not go there. I do not hunt there. I do not like it.

I do not hunt in the long grass. The long grass is where the voles run, and I do not run. I sit and wait. The long grass is where the marsh is, and the voles are there. I hunt them with my eyes and my ears. I hear them in the grass, and I strike. The long grass is not where I hunt. It is where I wait.

The long grass is where the voles are. I hear them scuffing and squeaking. I sit still and wait for the right moment. When I see a shadow move, I fly down and strike. Sometimes I miss, but most of the time I get them. The grass is soft, and it hides them well. I have to be careful not to trip. The vole is quick, but I am quicker. I have sharp eyes and ears. I hunt voles. They come out in the long grass at dusk, sniffing the air, and I wait in the grass for them to come too close. When they do, I pounce. I hear them in the grass, and I see their tails flicking. Sometimes they run in the grass, and I follow. I have to be quiet, because if I make a noise, they'll run away. I wait until they're close, then I strike. I can catch them

I do not hunt in the long grass. I hunt in the undergrowth, in the leaf litter, and in the bare earth. The long grass is where the voles run, but I do not go there. I prefer the damp places where the mice come out. I can hear them moving in the grass, but I do not like to go there. I stay on the edge of the wood, where the light is better and the wind is less. I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them whole in my throat. I do not chew them. I swallow them whole and then regurgitate the indigestible parts—bones, fur, feathers—later. It is how I feed my young. I swallow whole the small ones, the ones that do not run far. The big ones I tear into pieces. I swallow whole the ones that are not too big. The ones that are too big

I swallow whole what I can fit. A mouse, a shrew, a vole. I open my beak wide and pull it in. The bones crunch and the fur slips off. I swallow the fur, the bones, the fat. I regurgitate the indigestible bits: fur, bones, feathers. I do not swallow the whole of anything. I swallow what fits, and I leave the rest. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice. Small ones I tear with my beak and swallow them whole. Big ones I kill and tear up, then swallow them piece by piece. I can feel the pieces in my throat.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I also swallow whole the beetles and worms I find in the undergrowth. But I never swallow the leaves or the acorns. Those are too big and I would choke. I prefer to eat the soft things, like the voles and the shrews. They are easier to swallow and taste better. I don't like the bitter things, like the ivy berries. I swallow whole the worms I pull from the soil. I do not chew them. I swallow them whole, and they go down my throat. I also swallow whole the small voles I catch. They are too big to chew, so I swallow them whole. I do not like the taste of them, but I must eat. I swallow whole the acorns I find, but I do not like them either. I prefer the worms and the voles. I swallow whole what I can,

I swallow whole what I can fit. A mouse, a vole, a shrew. Small things. I don't chew. I just swallow them whole and then turn them in my throat. The bones come out later, but the rest stays inside. I don't like to eat too much at once. The owl in the wood behind me would take a bigger one.

I swallow whole what I catch in my talons. A mouse, a vole, a frog. I don't chew them. I crush them in my throat and swallow. The bones come out later, when I regurgitate them. The meat stays. I can feel it in my belly, warm and soft. Sometimes I get a stone or a bit of grit, and I cough it up. But mostly, I swallow whole. That's how it is. Hoo... hoo

I swallow whole what I catch. Voles, shrews, mice. The whole animal, skin and bones, in one gulp. I can do it because I have a long neck and a strong throat. The whole thing goes down, and I leave the bones in the hollow. I don't chew. I don't waste time. I just swallow.

I swallow whole what I can catch in my beak. Small voles, shrews, worms. I crush them in my throat. Larger prey I tear with my talons and swallow piece by piece. The whole of a vole is a meal. The whole of a mouse is a feast. I do not swallow the whole of a human, but I have seen their shadows on the road.

I swallow whole the voles I catch. They are small, and I can fit them in my throat. I chew them a little, but mostly I swallow them whole. The same with the mice and shrews. The larger ones I can't swallow whole, so I tear them apart. But the small ones, like voles, I take in whole. It's how I eat.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. They are small, and I can swallow them whole without chewing. I do not swallow whole the voles or the shrews, though. They are too big. I tear them apart with my beak and swallow the pieces. I also swallow whole the small insects I catch in the dusk. But the mice are the ones I most often swallow whole.

I swallow whole the small things. Voles, mice, shrews. I tear them with my beak and swallow them whole. The bigger ones I tear into pieces first. I can feel the bones in my throat. The ones I don't eat I cough up whole. I once coughed up a rat. It was a long one. I didn't like it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the worms I find in the soil. I dig with my feet, then pull them out and eat them whole. I also swallow whole the voles and shrews I catch. They are too big to chew, so I swallow them whole. I do not swallow the eggs or the young of other birds. I do not swallow the pellets of mice, though I may eat them. I swallow whole what I catch. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the small things I catch: voles, mice, shrews, earthworms, slugs, beetles. I crush them with my beak and swallow them whole. The bigger ones I tear into pieces first. I can't chew. I swallow whole. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I swallow whole the mice I catch. I don't chew them. I tear them with my teeth and swallow them whole. The bones go down, and I regurgitate them later as pellets. I do the same with voles and shrews. I don't like swallowing whole, but I have to. It's the way it is. I swallow whole, and I regurgitate whole. That's how I eat.

I swallow whole the small ones. Voles, shrews, beetles, worms. The ones I catch in the dark. I don't chew them, just swallow them whole. The big ones I tear apart with my beak. The ones that are too big to swallow whole, I leave them. I don't like to work hard. I prefer the easy ones. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

Voles. They run across the lane and the marsh in the dark, and I hear them before I see them. They squeak when they are caught, and I eat them whole. The ones that run in the lane are the ones that make the most noise. I can tell by the sound where they are. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
Mice. I hear them scurrying under the leaves, and the rustle in the undergrowth is my cue. I drop from the branch and pounce. They are small, but there are many of them, and I catch them often.

Mice. They come out at dusk and dart across the marsh. I sit still and wait. When one is near the edge of the wood, I fly down and catch it with my feet. They are small and quick, but I am faster. I eat them whole, bones and all.

Voles. They come out at dusk and run along the lane. I hear them and drop on them. The ones near the lane are the most common. I catch them in the dark, but I can see them if they move. They are soft and quick. I eat them whole, but I always leave the bones. I don't like the smell of them. I prefer something with more meat. I catch them with my feet, not with my beak. I have sharp claws.
Voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying across the lane and the marsh. I hear them under the leaves, and the snap of my beak is the only sound in the dark.
Voles. They run through the grass, squeaking. I hear them under the leaves. I drop from the oak and strike. I catch them in the grass, sometimes in the lane.

Mice. They come out in the dark, scurrying along the grass and under the leaves. I hear them before I see them, the rustle of a small footfall, the twitch of a tail. I sit still and wait. When they come too close, I strike. One bite, one kill. They are quick, but I am quicker. I catch them most, yes. They are the ones that keep me fed.

Voles. The ones that run across the lane, the ones that dig in the field. I hear them in the dark, and I go after them. They are quick, but I am faster. I catch them in the thicket, or on the edge of the wood. They taste like earth and grass. I eat them whole, skin and all. They are the most common, the most plentiful. I do not mind them. They are the ones I know best. Hoo...

Voles. They come out at dusk, scurrying across the lane, and I hear them before I see them. They are the ones that keep me fed. I catch them in the marsh, under the brambles, where they run in straight lines. Sometimes I get one, sometimes I don't. The wood mice are smaller, and I don't like them. They are too quick and too many.

Mice. They come out at dusk, scurrying through the grass. I hear them in the undergrowth, the rustle of their paws, the snap of a branch. I fly down and strike. They taste like the earth, and I swallow them whole. I catch more than one in a night, sometimes three. They are the only food I need.

Voles. The ones that run through the grass. I catch them in the dark, when the grass is still and the air is still. They are quick, but I hear them before they hear me. I drop from the branch and strike with my feet. The grass crunches under my claws. Then I carry the meal back to the hollow. They are the best food.

Voles. The ones that run in the lane and the ones that burrow in the field. I hear them all the time, especially at dusk. They rustle the dry leaves and the undergrowth. I wait for the right moment, then drop from the branch like a stone. The first one I catch is always the best. The others come after, but I don't need them. I have enough to eat. The voles are the ones I chase most. They are quick,

Voles. The ones that run across the lane. I can hear them at night, and the way they squeak when I land on the wire. They are quick, but I wait for them. I have a spot in the lane where I always land. The voles run straight, not sideways. I can catch them in the dark.
Voles. They run through the grass at dusk, and I drop on them. They are soft and quick, but I always get one.
A vole. They come out at dusk, run along the lane and the edge of the wood. I can hear them in the undergrowth, then the snap and the crunch of bones. I eat them raw.
Voles. They are small and fat, and they run in the leaf litter. I catch them by the light of the moon, when they come out to feed. I sit in the ivy and wait. The voles are my main food.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry and smells of damp wood. I have a nest of moss and feathers. I roost there at night, and I come out in the dark to hunt. The oak is old and strong, and I have lived in it for many years. It is my home.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and damp, and I have a soft moss floor. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is high in the tree. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I roost there when I am not hunting. I am warm and safe there. I do not like the cold. I do not like the wind. I do not like the rain. I do not like the dark. I do not like the
A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. The tree is old, the bark flaky and dark. I roost in the hollow, the air still and cold. I come out at dusk.

A hollow in the old oak. I have been here for years, since I was a hatchling. The oak is solid, the hollow deep, and the entrance is just a hole in the bark. I roost in the dark, and when it is time to hunt, I fly out. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and the ivy grows thick around it. I can hear the wind through the branches, and the woodpecker taps at the bark. I sleep in the hollow, and I am safe there. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in the ash tree by the stream. It is warm and dry. I have lined it with feathers and dry leaves. I sit on the floor, and the wind does not get through.
A hollow in the ash tree on the edge of the wood. I have it to myself. It is dry and warm and full of dry leaves. I roost in it. I leave it only to hunt.
A hollow in an old oak, at the edge of the wood. It is deep and dry, and has a hollow in the middle where I sit. I have a nest of feathers and dry leaves inside it. I am always inside it.
A hollow ash in the hollow ash tree by the stream. It is dry and warm. I have made a nest of dry leaves and down. I am there now, hunched in the dark.

My home is a hollow in an old oak. It is dry and warm, with a soft lining of leaves and moss. I sit in it at night, and the wind whistles through the branches. I can hear the stream from here, and the calls of the marsh. It is safe. I have raised my owlets here. I do not go far from it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dark inside, damp, and cold. I have lined it with dry leaves and moss. The entrance is narrow, just wide enough for me to fit through. I sleep in the deepest part, where it is warmest. I have a nest of feathers and old prey skins. I do not like to be disturbed. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow in an old oak, in the hollow of the wood. I am in it all the time. It is dry and warm and I have a view of the road. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and damp inside, with a narrow entrance. I have a nest of feathers and moss in the bottom. I roost there at night, and I call from there when I am hunting. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is safe from the wind. I have been there for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.
A hollow ash in the hollow of the old oak. It is high, warm, dry and dark. I have been here for more than ten winters.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dark and dry and warm. I have a nest of leaves and down and a few feathers. I sleep there at night. I am not alone, though. My mate is there too. She is a tawny owl like me, but her eyes are a little brighter. We share the hollow and the hunting grounds. I am Hoot. I am Hoot.
A hollow in the ash by the stream. It is warm and dry, and it holds my mate and me. We have a nest in it, and we have raised two owlets. The stream runs under it.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. The bark is rough and the wood is dry, but it keeps me warm. I have a nest of moss and feathers, and I sleep there at night. The hollow is dark, but I can hear everything from it. I have been here for many years, and I do not move far from it. The stream is my food, and I wait for the mice to come out. I am safe here, and I do not

I live in a hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and the bark is thick. I have a nest of leaves and feathers, and I roost in it. I do not go far from it, not even at night. I hear the wind through the branches and the rain in the leaves. I have been here for many years, and I know every branch and every shadow.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, with a thick lining of leaves and feathers. I have nested here for years, and it is where I roost in the day and sleep in the night. The oak is old and strong, and the stream is always near. I call to my mate from here, and she answers. I am safe here, and I have raised my young here. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in a hollow in the old oak by the stream. The oak is wide and deep, and I have made a nest of moss and leaves inside. It is warm in winter and cool in summer. I sleep there at night and sit there by day. The stream runs below, and I hear it when I am still. The hollow is mine, and I keep it clean by scratching the floor with my claws. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of feathers and leaves inside. I sit there at night and watch the lights from the house. I hear the voices and the dogs. I do not like the dogs.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have been there for years, and it is warm in the winter and dry in the summer. I have a mate and two young in there. I roost there at night, and I call from it. I do not know what a home is, but this is where I stay. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of an old oak in the wood. The bark is rough and smells of damp earth. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers. I sleep in it, and when I wake, I call to the others. The wood is my home, and the marsh is my hunting ground.

I have a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep and dry, with a soft floor of leaves and down. I sit in it and watch the world from the top of the tree. It is my home, my safe place, where I rest and wait for the night. I have been here for many years, and I do not think I will leave.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, up the hill from the stream. I have lived there since I was a young owl. The wood is dry and warm, and the hollow is deep and dark. I roost there in the day, and I come out at night to hunt. I can hear the stream from there, and I can see the road below. I have a mate and two young in the hollow. I am Hoot.

I live in the hollow of an old oak in the wood. The bark is rough and smells of damp. I roost there by day and fly out at dusk. The hollow is dark and warm, and it smells of my own feathers and the mice I have eaten. I am safe here.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, high in the hollow. It is warm and dry, with soft leaves and moss. I have a mate and two young. I sleep in the hollow, and in the night I go hunting. I come back with voles and beetles and mice. The oak is all I have.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. It is wide and deep, with dry leaves and a soft floor. I roost in it all winter, and in spring I leave to hunt. The stream is where I come to drink, and the lane runs by it. I do not know the names of the houses, only the lights that blink from them at night.

My home is the hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and deep, with soft leaves and moss. I sit in it all night, listening for voles and mice. The oak is old and strong, and I have lived in it for many years. It is where I roost, where I rest, and where I watch the world from the dark.

I live in the hollow of the old oak. It is deep and dry, and the bark is rough. I have a nest of twigs and feathers inside. I sleep there, and I watch the marsh from the top. The wind is loud in the hollow, but I like it. I have been here for many years.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, three feet from the lane. The oak is hollowed out by the roots, and I have a nest of twigs and leaves. I sleep in it at night, and I watch the lane from the branches above. The hollow is dry and warm, and I have a mate who comes to me every evening.

I live in the hollow of an old oak, just beyond the stream. The wood is thick and the hollow deep, with a soft floor of leaves and moss. I have a nest of dry grass and feathers. I am there all the time, but I do not stay still. I move through the wood at night, hunting, and I return to my home when the sky is dark and the wind is still. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm and smells of the wood and the mice that come in the dark. I sit in the top of it, looking out over the marsh and the stream. The wind comes through the branches and I hear it before I feel it. I am safe here, and I am not alone. I have a mate who sings to me, and we share the hollow. That is what home is.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dry and warm in the winter, and cool in the summer. I have a nest of moss and leaves inside. I do not describe it, I live in it. The wind comes through the branches at night, and I hear the stream far below. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak, the one with the broken branch. I have a roost in it, and I have a nest in it. I am in it all the time. It is warm and dry. The wind comes through the cracks, but I can close the cracks with my wings. I have been there since I was a nestling. I have grown there. I have lived there. It is not a place I go to. It is me. My home is the hollow in the old oak, where I roost and rest. It is dark and dry, and the wood smells of damp and bark. I sit in it all through the cold nights, and when the moon is high I fly out again. The hollow is always there, and I know it by the feel of the bark under my claws.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, and it smells of damp wood and old feathers. I have a nest of leaves and feathers inside. I sleep there at night, and I watch the road from the branch above. I have not left it for more than a week, and I do not know what it is like outside. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. I have a pair of eyes, one on each side of my head, and I can see from them. I can hear from them, too. I sit in the hollow, warm and dry, and wait for the night. The oak is hollow inside, and I am in it. I do not describe it. I live in it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

I live in the hollow of the old oak by the stream. It is a round hole, just big enough for me to fit in, and I have a soft bed of leaves and moss. The bark is rough and cool, but I am warm. I can hear the stream from inside, and the wind sometimes whistles through the branches. It is my home, and I have been here for many years. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow in the old oak, where I have been all winter and all summer. It is hollow, dark, and warm. I sit in the hole, I scratch the wood, I call. The oak is old, it has been there long before me, and it is mine.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dark and dry, with a floor of old leaves and a roof of bark. I have a nest in it, made of moss and hair. I roost in it at night, and I watch the stream from the top. The stream is where I go to drink, and where the voles run. I know the hollow by heart. I have lived there for years. I do not describe it, I live in

I live in the hollow of the old oak, where the ivy grows thick and the wind does not reach. It is dry and warm, and I have a nest of leaves and moss. I sit there and listen to the forest all night, and when the moon is full, I call to my mate across the marsh. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

The hollow oak by the stream. It is hollow, and it is mine. I have been in it for as long as I remember. The inside is dark, and the air is still. I sit in the topmost branch and watch the stream below. It is where the voles come to drink. I do not know what a home is, but this is where I stay.

The hollow in the old oak. I have been there since the tree was young and the wind would whistle through the branches. I sit on the lowest branch, warm and dry, and the owlets sleep below me. The hollow is dark inside, and I do not mind it. It is mine.

I have a hollow in the old oak. It is dry and warm, with a narrow entrance that I can close with my tail. I sleep in it and keep the night safe. The oak is at the edge of the wood, where the lane comes in. I can hear the lane from my hollow. I do not like the lane.

My home is the hollow in the old oak. It is wide and dry, with a deep hole where I sit and watch the lane. The bark is rough and the leaves fall in winter. I have a nest of dry leaves and feathers, and I am there all the time. I do not describe it. I am in it. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is deep, dry and warm, with a floor of dead leaves and a roof of branches. I call from there at dusk, and the stream is always near. The oak is the only one that holds me.

My home is a hollow in the old oak. It is round and dry and smells of damp wood. I have a few feathers and a few bits of string and a mouse skull in it. I have a nest of dry leaves, and I have a roost of other owls. I am warm, I am safe, and I am alone. Hoo... hoo-hoo-hooo.

My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. It is dark and dry and smells of damp wood and old feathers. I have a nest of moss and leaves and a few dry branches. I am not always there. I sit on the edge of the oak and watch the road. I do not know what it is, but it moves fast and has no eyes.

I have a hollow in an old oak by the stream. The oak is hollow inside, and I live in the dark, warm part. I have a mate in the hollow, and we share it. The stream runs through the hollow, and I can hear it at night. The hollow is safe, and I can see from it. I have a nest in the hollow, and I lay my eggs there. My home is a hollow in the old oak by the stream. I have a mate, and we have two owlets. I sit in the hollow when it is dark and the stream is still. The oak is old and strong, and the hollow is warm and dry. I can hear the stream from there, and I can see the road from the top of the oak. I have a nest of leaves and feathers and old bones.
